Hook: This series began in a city. In 1845 Frédéric Bastiat looked at Paris, a million people who would all go hungry within days if supplies stopped, and wondered why they slept peacefully. How does each succeeding day manage to bring to this gigantic market just what is necessary, neither too much nor too little? Part one's answer was prices. Sixty-six parts since have asked what else it takes: institutions, money, banks, states, and the evidence to tell which claims are true.

This part ends in a city too. On the fifth of January 2025, New York began charging nine dollars to drive into Manhattan below 60th Street in the day, two dollars twenty-five at night: the first price on entering a downtown in the United States, and William Vickrey's idea of Part fifteen, put into law. On an average weekday about 492 thousand vehicles still enter. A year in, the state said 11 percent fewer vehicles were entering, and 550 million dollars had been raised for transit. Is that right? What did the charge do, to traffic, to buses, to when people travel? This last part carries one question from an idea to a paper, with everything the series has built.

The question of the part: how is a new piece of economics made? It starts with a question that matters, can be answered, and has not been. Then the data, described before anything is estimated. A design, with its threats written down before the results are seen. A model, the smallest that speaks to the estimates, and a counterfactual: a policy that was not tried. And, because this is the last part, the series' accounts, closed.
Economics, Built. Part sixty-eight: the dissertation.

Part sixty-seven asked how much of economics is true. This part makes a piece of it. By the end you will know how to choose a question, find its data and describe them first; how to choose a design and list its threats before you see a result; what New York's charge did to traffic, to buses and to the clock, and what the design cannot say; how to build the smallest model that speaks to the estimates, and carry its uncertainty into a policy that was not tried; and what the series' Facts, Dials and Tableau finally show.
Data: The data come first, and they are public. Hourly crossings of the transit authority's ten bridges and tunnels since 2019; two of the tunnels lead straight into the zone. Entries into the zone every ten minutes, by type of vehicle and entry point, which exist only since the charge began. Miles driven each day in the zone and on its two free highways, since 2024. And bus speeds, route by route, inside and outside the business district, since 2023. Each file was reduced by a query written down in the Data Room, so anyone can rebuild it.

Describe before estimating. Here is every day since the charge began: the vehicles entering the zone. Weekdays, in gold, sit in a band near half a million; weekends and holidays fall below. On an average weekday 492 thousand vehicles enter, and 56 percent of all entries are cars, pickups and vans. Notice what this chart cannot show: there is no before. Entries were first counted when the cameras started charging, so this file alone can never say what the charge did.

The crossings have a before. Weekday traffic by month since 2019, each group indexed to its 2019 level: in red, the two tunnels whose Manhattan-bound lanes lead into the zone; in blue, 13 directions of crossings elsewhere in the city. First the pandemic's hole in 2020, and a recovery, stronger in the tunnels. Then something to write down before estimating anything: from 2023 the tunnels' traffic slips back relative to the other crossings, two years before the charge. Whatever design we use will have to deal with it.
PlayIt: Chapter four. Play it: predict the result.

Your turn, as the dissertation's first reader. Write down your predictions before the estimates arrive; a forecast written first cannot be revised afterwards. One: in 2025, how did traffic through the two tunnels change, relative to the other crossings? Two: how did bus speeds inside the business district change, relative to routes outside? Three: on weekdays, how do car entries in the ten minutes after nine at night compare with the ten minutes before, when the toll falls from nine dollars to two twenty-five? Pause, and choose.

The answers, in the order the next chapters will earn them. One: B. Relative to the other crossings, tunnel traffic fell by 2.6 percent, and by about 1.2 percent once the tunnels' earlier drift is taken out. Two: B. Buses inside the district got 1.3 percent faster than buses outside. Three: C. Car entries jump by about 26 percent the moment the toll drops. The largest effect is not on whether people drive, but when.
Estimates: Chapter five. The estimates, and what they cannot say.

The crossings first. Each bar is one month: the tunnels' year-on-year change minus the other crossings', in percent. The grey and blue bars are 2023 and 2024, before any charge: the placebos. They are not zero. The tunnels were losing ground by 1.4 percent a year before anything happened. In 2025, the red bars, the gap averages 2.6 percent. Net of the drift, the charge's effect on the tunnels is about 1.2 percent, with a standard error of 0.6 percent: small, and only just distinguishable from zero. The orange bars of 2026 compare two charged years, and look like the drift again.

Then buses and miles. At the weekday peak, buses inside the business district averaged 9.49 miles an hour in 2024 and 9.67 in 2025. Against buses outside, the gain is 1.3 percent, where the placebo year shows 0.1 percent. Miles driven in the zone fell 3.9 percent, and on its two free highways 2.4 percent. Fewer miles, slightly faster buses, a small effect on the tolled tunnels: a modest, measurable change.

So which is it? The state reported eleven percent fewer vehicles entering the zone, against a projection of what entries would have been without the charge. This study finds 3.9 percent fewer miles driven in the zone than a year before, and small effects against comparison crossings and routes. They need not conflict. Entries are not miles; a projection is a model of the counterfactual, a comparison group is another; and the free bridges are in neither. And no design here can say how many trips were given up rather than moved, who paid, or what a higher toll would do. That takes a model.
Clock: Chapter six. The clock: a discontinuity in time.

Now the clock. On the left, cars entering the zone every ten minutes on an average weekday, from seven to eleven at night, over 485 weekdays. The toll falls from nine dollars to two twenty-five at nine o'clock. A line through the blocks on each side, and the gap where they meet: entries jump by 26 percent the moment the toll falls. In the first hour after nine, about 2,361 more cars enter than the evening's trend predicts. On the right, the morning, when the toll rises at five. Drivers crowd in before it, and entries fall by 31 percent at the stroke of five: about 4,354 fewer cars in the next hour than the early-morning trend.

What does the clock show? It is the cleanest result in the study: nothing else changes at nine o'clock, so the jump is the price. But read it carefully. A discontinuity at a cutoff measures retiming: the driver who waits until five past nine still comes. It cannot tell how many trips were given up altogether. What it does measure is Vickrey's point: a price that varies by time of day spreads the peak.
Model: The designs say what happened. To ask what a different toll would do, we need a model, and the rule is to use the smallest one that speaks to the estimates. Two pieces. First, time per trip rises with traffic, along the curve road engineers have used since the 1960s. Its slope comes from the data: miles in the zone fell 3.9 percent, bus travel time fell 1.9 percent, so each percent less traffic saves about 0.48 percent of time. Second, demand for trips falls with their full price: the toll, the time, and everything else a trip costs. The numbers we do not observe are assumptions, written on the screen: 3 miles in the zone at 10 miles an hour, time worth 20 dollars an hour, half a typical wage as in Part fifty-eight, other costs of 25 dollars. Then the observed fall in traffic, when the price rose by the toll and fell a little with the faster trip, gives the elasticity: minus 0.15. Driving into Manhattan is very inelastic.

With both pieces, the model gives traffic at any toll. It passes through the one point we observed, nine dollars, by construction. Everywhere else, the model is speaking, not the data: at fifteen dollars, the original plan, traffic would be about 5.9 percent below its uncharged level at the central assumptions.

The model also prices the thing a congestion charge is for. One more car adds a little delay to every other car. Added up, that is the marginal external cost of a trip: the time elasticity, times the trip's time, times what time is worth. At the central assumptions, about 2.90 dollars a trip. That is Pigou's tax of Part fifteen, for drivers' time alone. It leaves out bus riders, whose time the faster buses save; pedestrians; safety; noise; emissions; and the peak hour, where one more car costs far more than the day's average. So the narrow model alone cannot justify nine dollars. The case rests on what it leaves out, and on the revenue for transit, which the law intended. Saying so is part of the paper.
Counterfactual: Chapter eight. The counterfactual: the fifteen-dollar plan.

Good counterfactuals are ones someone needs. This one has a date. In June 2024 a fifteen-dollar charge, due to begin on the thirtieth, was paused weeks before it started. In November a nine-dollar charge was approved instead, rising to twelve dollars in 2028 and fifteen in 2031. So the question writes itself: what would fifteen dollars have done, and what will the next steps do?

And the answer must carry its uncertainty. Two kinds: the estimates themselves, each with a standard error, and the assumptions, each with a range. Draw both two thousand times, recalibrate the model each time, and report the median with the range that holds ninety percent of the draws. At fifteen dollars, traffic in the zone would be about 5.9 percent below its uncharged level, somewhere between 4.5 and 7.3 percent. Trips in the zone would be about 2.6 percent faster. And the delay a car imposes on other drivers is worth between 1.3 and 6.0 dollars, a range wide enough to say what matters: the narrow case for fifteen dollars is weaker than the case for nine, and both rest on costs the model leaves out.
Writing: Chapter nine. Writing it, and the referees.

A paper is read from its introduction, so the introduction is the argument in miniature. First the question and why it matters. Then what the paper does. Then what it finds, with the numbers. Then the honest part: why the answer differs from the official figure, and what the designs cannot say. Then the model, the counterfactual, and what they leave out. A talk follows the same five steps, in twenty minutes, with one picture for each.

Then the referees, the colleagues an editor asks to find what is wrong. The first asks whether the tunnels' drift is the pandemic's long tail, and whether the result depends on which years are the placebos. The reply does the work: estimate the drift from 2023 and 2024, then from 2024 alone, and report both. The second asks the hardest question: how much traffic moved to the free bridges, which this data cannot see? The honest reply is that this data cannot bound it; a model can show which way the bias runs, and the paper must say so. Most of a paper's quality is made in replies like these.

And the replies, in numbers. The paper's estimate: net of the drift measured over 2023 and 2024, 1.2 percent. With the drift measured from 2024 alone, as the first referee asked, 0.9 percent. Dropping the two bridges whose traffic also flows into Manhattan from the comparison group, 1.4 percent. Every answer sits inside the main estimate's interval. The result is small and steady; what remains uncertain is diversion, and the paper says so.
Island: Chapter ten. The same paper on the Island.

This series has always checked a method where the truth is known. So run the same paper on the Island: two tolled crossings, eight others, a shared season, and a charge that truly removes four percent of the tolled crossings' traffic. When the crossings would have moved in parallel, the method finds 4 percent on average: right, though any single Island can miss by a couple of points. When thirty percent of the lost trips divert to the comparison crossings, the comparison group grows and the method overstates the effect: 4.3 percent. When the tolled crossings were already drifting down one and a half percent a year, the plain comparison finds 5.5 percent, the effect plus the drift. Subtracting the placebo year recovers 4 percent, and more precisely. That is the correction chapter five applied to New York, checked where the answer is known.
Facts: Chapter eleven. Agora against the Facts.

Part one fixed 36 Facts that any account of an economy has to reproduce, from Engel's law to the child penalty. Each had three columns: your guess, the data, and Agora, the economy the series built, filled in by the part that built the mechanism. Here is the whole list. 33 of the 36 are reproduced: Agora's households smooth consumption, its firms set sticky prices, its traders converge, its bidders suffer the winner's curse, its growth is flat for millennia and then takes off, its banks lend into crises, its cities and incomes follow Zipf and Pareto.

And the 3 that stayed open. Firm sizes follow Zipf's law; the random growth that produces it was built for cities in Part thirty-seven, and never run for firms. Expansions are long and recessions short; the equilibrium cycle of Part twenty-nine is symmetric, and a switching model only describes the asymmetry. The yield curve inverts before most recessions; Part fifty-seven measured it, but no part built the expectations that would produce it. Three Facts the series could show and not explain. A scorecard that admits its gaps is worth more than one that hides them.
Dials: The Dials, for the last time. Each act opened Dials as it met numbers the world has to supply, stacked here by act and coloured by status. Of the 93, 20 are settled within a range, 35 depend on the setting, 36 are contested and 2 cannot be identified with the data we have. Settled answers are rare in every act, never more than two Dials in three and usually far fewer; the acts on markets and on money and the cycle are the most contested, and the graduate core opened none, since it built tools rather than measured the world. Most of what economics measures depends on where and when it is measured, and saying so is not a failure of the field but its main finding.

And the series' other ledger: Called it? 65 predictions made in advance by economists, officials and markets, each put beside what happened. 12 were right, 21 partly right, 28 wrong, and 4 are too early to say. Wrong is the commonest verdict, and fewer than one call in five was simply right. The lesson is not that economists should stop forecasting, but that a forecast should come with a range, and someone should keep score.
